newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Branson hopes to take off soon on balloon trip. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Branson hopes to take off soon on balloon trip. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson said on Tuesday he hoped to take off within hours from the ancient Moroccan city of Marrakesh in his attempt to become the first to fly around the world by balloon.
A planned dawn takeoff was delayed by the complexities of filling the giant balloon with 1.1 million cubic feet (30,000 cubic metres) of helium and hot air.
Branson, 46, warned of a possible delay of some hours late on Monday night, telling reporters: "It is a complicated operation to assemble the huge balloon...In fact, it takes more time."

A new time of between 0730 and 0900 GMT appeared unlikely to be met because of what co-pilot Rory McCarthy called "minor technical problems". But Branson later told the U.S. network CNN on Tueday morning that he hoped to take off within a couple of hours.

McCarthy, who was to have made up the trio of balloonists with Branson and Per Lindstrand, later had to pull out of the trip because of suspected pneumonia. He was replaced by Alex Ritchie, 50, who was on standby as reserve co-pilot.
McCarthy told reporters at the airbase he was very disappointed after two years of preparations. "There will be no flight like this one in future. I wish them a good flight."

Early on Tuesday the white balloon appeared about half inflated, lying in the middle of a military airfield under a clear, cloudless sky. Branson had arrived at the airfield and was with his technicians.
Members of his team said there were plans to attach three massive cans, one red and two yellow, to the accommodation capsule to advertise the tycoon's "Virgin Coke" drink.
The weather in Marrakesh, chosen as an ideal spot to enter the southern jet stream, was reported perfect for takeoff.
Twelve rods and three "umbilical cords" are tethering the balloon. At takeoff, the rods will be automatically disengaged, and finally the cords cut.

At 194.8 feet (59.38 metres) tall -- roughly the height of a 12-storey building -- the balloon was constructed of fabric specifically designed for the project. The laminated envelope is made from a high-tenacity polyamide fabric coated with a polyurethane compound.
The balloon, carrying Branson, head of the Virgin group of companies, and his co-pilots, should soar to 30,000 feet (10,000 metres) to pass over the nearby snowcapped Atlas Mountains.
It will then head east over North Africa, Saudi Arabia, India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and then across the United States, with touchdown planned for Oxfordshire in southern England.
Branson expects the trip to take 14 to 21 days, with what he termed "a realistic time" of 18 days.
Speed is essential as Branson is racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset and a two-man team planning a launch from St. Louis, Missouri in the United States.
"I am aware of the competition but I can assure you that we will be one or two days ahead of Steve Fosset," Branson said.
